parts: Lesson 5: A Tiger Comes to Town (I) — Summary

This extract from R.K. Narayan's story is told by a runaway circus tiger. Through the tiger's eyes we see how foolish and fearful human beings can be, and how wrongly they judge animals. The story asks us to treat animals with compassion and to understand that animals too have feelings.

When the tiger enters Market Road, people run for their lives: shutters are pulled down and people hide in drains, on trees and behind pillars — 'the population was melting out of sight'. At the circus the tiger had seen people sitting calmly while he cowered before the Captain's whip, so he had thought humans were strong and fearless. Now they run from him 'like a herd of deer', though he has no intention of attacking them.

A tailor abandons his machine and shuts himself in a cupboard, wailing 'Won't someone shoot that tiger?' A prisoner escapes when his two constables flee, leaving him in handcuffs. The tiger tears a horse from a jutka and enjoys the passengers spilling out. Sheer hopelessness seizes the townspeople: all doors and windows are shut, bolted and sealed; some think he is an extraordinary creature who might pass through walls. The tiger wonders why a simple tiger should have any interest in them, 'either to destroy or to safeguard'.

At a restaurant the coffee drinkers and tiffin-eaters sit still, moaning; the cashier hugs his cash box, afraid even to breathe. The tiger wants to assure them, 'Don't fear, I am not out to trouble you.' He is eleven feet from tip to tail and is not hungry — he had found a 'green pasture full of food' on the way. 'Tigers attack only when they feel hungry, unlike human beings who kill one another without purpose or hunger.'

Schools close hurriedly; children run 'helter-skelter', delighted — 'No school, no school. Tiger, Tiger!' The tiger follows them into the school, walks into the Headmaster's room — the dignified Headmaster jumps on the table and heaves himself into the attic — and lies down on the cool stone floor with his head under the desk to sleep. While he sleeps, the room is locked and watched.

When a teacher calls him a 'brute', his Master pushes through the crowd and scolds them: 'Never use the words beast or brute. They're ugly words coined by man in his arrogance.' When someone asks, 'Who are you?', the Master replies that it is a profound question — he has been trying to find out who he is all his life: 'Are you sure you know who you are?'

Humans judge animals by fixed ideas and panic needlessly; animals are not cruel without reason; humans can be more violent than animals; the Master stands for respect and compassion for all creatures. The story is full of gentle humour and irony.
